REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN TORONTO "STAR" OF MARCH 8
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, though I am happy to say I seldom have to do so. In last evening's Toronto Star I read an article headed, "Say M.P. in hospital but don't tell him". It refers to a rumour that apparently was circulated both here and in Toronto to the effect that I was ill. I have not been ill in forty to fifty years, though I did have a cold about ten days ago. I am not criticizing the Star for referring to a rumour, but the last part of this article reads:
Today there was a new report: Mr. MacNicol had been rushed to the hospital.
If the House of Commons is looked upon as a hospital-for I rush here daily-that statement is true; but I am happy to say I have never felt better.
On the order for motions:

subsubtopic: PROCEDURE FOLLOWED IN TABLING AND GAZETTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table returns to orders passed on February 24 and March 7 on questions asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in respect to orders in council. The question of February 24 was:
How many orders in council passed since July 1, 1948, as at the 18th of February, 1949, were not (a) tabled; (b) published in the Canada Gazette?
The answer is: There were 7,005 orders in council passed between July 1, 1948, and February 18, 1949-including 4,215 minutes of treasury board-of which 6,777 were not tabled and 6,728 were not published in the Canada Gazette.
The second order passed on March 7 read:
1.	How many orders in council were passed between (a) September 1, 1939, and September 1, 1945; (b) September 1, 1945, and date hereof?
2.	Of these orders in council, how many were passed under the provisions of the (a) War Measures
Vet; (b) the several emergency powers acts?
The answer is:
1.	Between September 1, 1939, and September 1, 1945, there were 55,559 orders in council; treasury boards (464) containing minutes totaling 34,988, making a grand total of 90,547.
Between September 1, 1945, and March 4, 1949, there were 19,098 orders in council; treasury boards (245) containing minutes totaling 35,737, or a grand total of 54,835.
2.	Orders in council referred to in 1 (a) and (b) passed under (a) the War Measures Act, 3,332; (b) (i) the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, 397; (ii) the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947, 21.
As promised in the house I am also tabling a descriptive list of the first hundred orders in council and minutes of treasury board passed since the beginning of the period mentioned in the hon. member's question. This list will indicate whether or not these orders in council and treasury board minutes have been tabled or gazetted or both. I am also tabling a summary of the first hundred orders in council and treasury board minutes passed since January 1, 1949. Taken together I think those two lists constitute a good cross-section of the various questions dealt with by order in council and treasury board minutes during the course of a year.
I think perhaps for the better information of hon. members it might be convenient to have these lists published as an appendix to Hansard of today, and if I have the consent of the house I would ask that this be done.

subsubtopic: PROCEDURE FOLLOWED IN TABLING AND GAZETTING
speechtext: In order, however, that the answers given in the past, and particularly the returns I have just tabled, may not prove to be misleading, I should like to avail myself of this opportunity to review briefly the procedure followed in the tabling and gazetting of orders in council, so that if this procedure is not satisfactory to the house it may be criticized and that criticism taken into consideration. In this matter, as in many others related to the business of government, the practice followed in Canada has been patterned very largely on United Kingdom constitutional procedures.

subsubtopic: PROCEDURE FOLLOWED IN TABLING AND GAZETTING
speechtext:
In
view of the lengthy and complete statement by the Prime Minister, may I, sir, with your leave and the leave of the house, direct his attention to one thing. As I understand it, in Great Britain a committee of the House of Commons has been given the responsibility of reviewing all orders in council as they are passed, for the purpose of bringing before the house any cases of invasion of rights or suspension of statutes by order in council. I was wondering whether the Prime Minister would consider the tabling of orders in council that are passed while parliament is in session. The members are in a very difficult position because legislative acts are performed under certain orders in council the tabling of which is not considered necessary. In view of the

attitude the Prime Minister has shown, and his desire to be of assistance to the house, would he agree to have these orders in council laid on the table of the house, having regard to the fact there is such a large number of them? It would be neither expensive nor difficult to do it. Hon. members would then know, as they advised their constituents, what the law or the practice is in respect to the various matters dealt with by order in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: PROCEDURE FOLLOWED IN TABLING AND GAZETTING
speechtext: If the hon. member will look at the two lists I have produced, he will perhaps come to the conclusion that it would be quite as convenient to have tabled monthly a full list of the orders in council of the preceding month, with the same kind of indications as are given in these lists. Then if in that list there was anything in which any hon. member was interested, he could ask to have the order in council tabled. But as about ninety per cent of the orders in council or minutes of the treasury board are merely administrative acts, I think it would be useless to table all of them and thus increase the store of parliamentary documents that the clerks of the house are obliged to take care of and keep for a long time after they have been tabled. Perhaps the matter could be referred to again. We want to make as full disclosure as will be of any use to anybody; but perhaps the hon. member will find that if he gets that kind of a list monthly he will have in it sufficient information to ask for any orders that were not already tabled and that might be of interest.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
subsubtopic: SUPPORT BOARD OF FISH IN DANGER OF SPOILAGE
speechtext:
I wish to make an announcement to the house about a serious situation which has developed in the inland fisheries of the prairie provinces, particularly Manitoba, and the action the government has authorized the fisheries prices support board to take to alleviate the problem.
Members will be aware that winter fishing operations in these northern lakes are carried on by fishermen taking the fish through the ice. The fish is frozen and stored at the lake under natural conditions until it is moved to market. Normally this movement to market takes care of all the fish before the spring breakup. This winter, largely because of the abnormal weather conditions and some softening of the export market, the Winnipeg trade has not been prepared to handle all the fish, and substantial quantities remain on the Ash-
Fisheries
ing grounds and at the railheads. This Ash must be moved immediately into refrigerated storage in Winnipeg to avoid spoilage.
Of the 2,800 Ashermen in Manitoba, many have suffered a serious decline in their incomes from this operation. This potential loss of food and the plight of the Ashermen was brought to the attention of the government through the Asheries prices support board by representatives of the Ashermen and the Ashing industry in Manitoba and the government of Manitoba which administers the Asheries of that province. The government has investigated and considered the problem and has authorized the board to stand ready to purchase such quantities of Ash as remain in Ashermen's hands or which are held on consignment by the Ash trade on behalf of the Ashermen.
The board has been authorized to offer to purchase the following species of Ash at speci-Aed prices, these being the species reported in Ashermen's hands and in danger of spoilage. The prices are on Winnipeg basis including freight and other handling charges, and are approximately eighty per cent of those which have been paid to date this year: whiteAsh, round, 13 cents per pound; saugers, round, 10 cents per pound; pike, (jacks), round, 6J cents per pound; pike (jacks), headless, 8| cents per pound; pickerel (yellows), round, 14 cents per pound; trout, round, 14 cents per pound; tullibee, round, 43,- cents per pound. The prices which the Ashermen may expect under this arrangement will be these prices less appropriate deductions for freight.
The board is immediately taking steps to set up the necessary machinery for handling this Ash, and will be making further announcements in this regard within the next day or two.

Mr. Frank T. Sian field (Colchesier-Hanis):
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few observations to add to what I said last evening before the house adjourned. I was referring then to the proposed St. Lawrence ship canal. I know this is a very important question, not only to the people of Canada but to the people of the United States as well. Being a good maritimer, however, I cannot do anything but take the position, which I think is very fair, that this canal will cost a great deal of money, of which the people of the mari-times will have to pay their share, and I think I am safe in saying they will not get any economic value whatever from the expenditure of that money on the construction of the proposed St. Lawrence canal. I for one could not vote for that project if we in the maritime provinces did not get something in return to offset that expenditure of money; and in that connection I suggest the bridge across the strait of Canso. I am not putting that forward as a threat at all, but being a good maritimer I figure it is nothing more than good business.
Now that Newfoundland has been brought into confederation the question of a bridge across the strait of Canso has become a matter of great importance. The people of Newfoundland have to get to and from that island, and that is going to be our responsibility; which makes the bridging of the strait of Canso very necessary indeed. The population of Nova Scotia and the maritimes as a whole has increased considerably, together with the rest of Canada; and if the people down there are to make a good living for themselves they must have fast, good transportation, which will enable them to compete

The Address-Mr. Drope on an equal basis with the rest of Canada. I do not intend to get into any argument on freight rates at this moment, but I must say that if we are to have the St. Lawrence canal deepened I do believe we in the maritimes should have the bridge across the strait of Canso.
There is only one other matter on which I want to speak; that is the reclaiming of our marshlands.
It is my understanding that something was to be done this session by the government by bringing down a bill for the reclaiming of the marshlands. We are very anxious to get the work started as early as possible this spring. As you know, a great many of the farms in Nova Scotia were abandoned during the war because of the high pay offered for other forms of work. We are very anxious to get these people back on the farms, but on good farms, not poor farms. Nothing would strengthen the economy of Nova Scotia more than getting twice as many people on the farms as we have now. The reclaiming of our marshlands would play a big part in any such program because they are rich lands and, worked in conjunction with the uplands, make good farms.
I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. McCubbin) whether or not the government contemplates bringing down a bill of that nature this session. It appears no one wishes to answer that question, Mr. Speaker. I see British Columbia is going ahead with some work of this nature-that is, the rediking of the Fraser river-and I realize that is very necessary; but so is the reclamation of our marshland in Nova Scotia. During the past four or five years many promises of help have been received in connection with reclaiming our marsh area; but so far nothing more has been done than merely helping, on a contributory basis, in repairing some breaks that come in the dikes. We should like to have some action started on the actual reclaiming of these rich marshlands this spring. With that, I shall conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker.

In the Globe and Mail, under date of March 5, I noticed an article the heading of which is "Unseemly Row." Some remarks are made in this article about the backbenchers of the Conservative party. I should like to say to this house that the backbenchers of the Conservative party are a fine body of men who observe the rules as well as any other group in the house. Just on this point, I should like to say that it makes little difference whether one is a backbencher or in the front benches. All the members of this house are on an equal footing, and all do their best to represent their constituencies. So far as I am concerned, I do not intend to take a back seat to anybody when it comes to talking about Northumberland county.
In this article to which I have referred, mention is made of the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) should have had more time allotted to him. The ministers of the crown are covered by the same rules as the other members of the house. The minister had already spoken for forty minutes-

speechtext:
Well, that is what the clock said, and there are three or four of them in this chamber. After having spoken for forty minutes, the last person to whom more time should be given is a minister. The ministers make statements every day and take up so much time that some of the ordinary members have few opportunities of saying anything. I am one of those who believe that not many people are converted in the last twenty minutes of a fifty minute sermon.
The tourist industry is something in which a great many citizens of Northumberland county are interested. I wish to congratulate the member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) on his approach to this problem. United States visitors to Canada should be encouraged. There is no better place in which to spend a holiday than in Canada, and no better place in Ontario than the county of Northumberland.
Much has been heard about the trans-Canada highway. No one need be in any doubt about where this party stands with regard to it, because our leader made our position quite clear. One of the first things we should have is a trans-Canada highway. I would say to the people of Canada that the sooner the leader of this party is Prime Minister, the sooner the construction of a trans-Canada highway will be undertaken.
The mail service is something that is of concern to all people. I should like to go on

record as saying that we are certainly living in the horse-and-buggy days so far as the postal services are concerned. The rural mail routes were laid out about thirty years ago. Everything in the country has changed during the last thirty years, and there have been shifts in the population. Very few changes have been made in the layout of the rural mail routes. The contracts for these routes still call for traveling at least four miles an hour, and that is about as fast as the mail seems to travel.
In my county there is one township in particular for which the mail has to be routed via Peterborough to reach the main line. Some of the boxholders tell me they could walk to Peterborough and back before a letter reaches that point. I brought this to the attention of the Post Office Department, but they are still fumbling around trying to ascertain whether anything can be done about it.
We are becoming so used to taxes on many things that nothing has been done about the tax on soft drinks and chocolate bars. I presume the government believes we are going to accept it as a permanent thing. It was put on during the war but, as most of us know, the war has been over for three or four years. The tax remains in effect, however.
I received a letter in my mail box just before coming into the chamber. It contains an offer from the film board to sell to members of the House of Commons and Senate, at the reduced rate of ten dollars, a film of the opening of parliament. It is said this is far below cost. Considering the amount of money the film board spends, I do not see any reason for offering this film to members of parliament at a reduced rate. Throughout the country the film board shows pictures, quite a number of which are enjoyable. It seems to me, however, that the people in charge of the making of some of these films are not too familiar with the agricultural scenes they are depicting.
Last week a picture was shown in the county of Northumberland depicting life on a modern dairy farm. The farmer put on his white overalls in the morning and went out to the barn. The stables had been all cleaned when he arrived, but I do not know who did that. Then the farmer proceeds to milk his fine herd of Holstein cows. After the milking he takes his herd of cows down to the pasture. The film continues by showing the work the farmer has to do during the day. Milking time comes around again and the farmer goes down to the pasture, but this time he returns with a herd of Ayrshire cows. It is wonderful how quickly the national film board can change the scene.
The Address-Mr. Drope
When we get talking about dairy cows, that brings us to a subject I think I know something about. I was interested in the return that was asked for by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) under date of February 23. I understand by this return that we imported into this country 15,680,000 pounds of butter. While some people have the idea that butter is too high in this country, I find when we get it over in Australia, New Zealand and Denmark a great deal more is paid for it than the farmers in Canada get. This butter is brought in, and in order to keep it at or below the ceiling it costs the taxpayers of Canada some $866,000. The actions of this government have certainly hit the farmers of this country. If reports are true that one out of six of our population is in some way interested in dairying, a good section of the population is certainly in for a bad time in the months ahead as a result of the action of the present government.
We make some cheese in this country and we seem to be exporting less of it each year.
I would suggest that, instead of putting the cheese up in the usual ninety-pound packages, we should put it up in smaller ones. A factory in my county is putting it up in smaller packages. The cheese could be put up in square packages so that it could be cut into pounds and half pounds, and wrapped in waxed paper. That is something that the average housewife will buy when she goes into the store, if it is wrapped up in a neat package. I believe we could sell more on the home market, which we all realize is the best market of all.
Income tax is the No. 1 problem of practically everybody you speak to. We are taxed to death. Nearly everyone is talking about the way the government is taking millions of dollars more than it needs. We heard that we had a surplus of $675 million. I wonder if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) credited all that against the debt of this country? If we have had all these surpluses that have been talked about, one would think that our debt would be reduced more than it is. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Henderson) the other day said something about these income tax forms. I do not want to repeat too much of what was said in that regard. I obtained a copy of that form, and I notice that it has been cut down from six pages to four. As to farmers, I think one page with about seven or eight questions would cover the whole thing, and that it would be something the average farmer would understand. If I were doing this, that is the way it would be. There is no need of all these questions. They are merely confusing. I often wonder if it does not cost about $10 to collect $5.

The Address-Mr. Drope
Food is a big problem in the world today. We in Canada probably have not so much to worry about; our biggest problem is finding satisfactory markets. But food is something that is of great concern to the world, and probably the peace of the world may depend upon it. Looking at the matter from the point of view of the world picture, at the present time we are up against a crisis. There is a world shortage of food amounting to famine in some lands, while in others there is a ration scale more skimpy than during the war. We in Canada are likely to think of hunger as a gnawing sensation that sends us with all speed to the nearest restaurant or to the kitchen; and we are surprised when we hear from a displaced person that chronic hunger does not make itself felt in the stomach but rather in the head. After a few months of inadequate diet your mind is robbed of all thought except that of finding something to eat. With that as your main desire, you cannot concentrate on producing goods for export, or on the moral issues in life.
Just last week I heard an appalling story of conditions in China. I heard it from a Canadian who had just returned after visiting that country. This person actually witnessed 89 children being picked up off the streets, they having died the night before from starvation. Twenty-six trucks were working in other parts of Shanghai at the same time and at the end of the trip dumped the dead bodies into an incinerator. That is only one illustration of the terrible misery in the world today. Can there be no solution to the problem of the distribution of food?
Solution of the problem emphasizes not only Ruskin's memorable dictum, "if you want food you must toil for it," but also the need for understanding, education and co-operation. This means that we must realize how utterly dependent we are upon the earth and its fruits. Canadians have a country which, by virtue of the gifts of Providence, is one of the largest suppliers of food to the world market. While many other countries have skidded far down the road toward national suicide by destroying the soil which alone makes possible their survival, we in Canada must constantly be on guard to protect our soil and expand its usefulness. Only a few inches of top soil stand between the human race and oblivion. It is the one natural resource, besides air and water, without which human life cannot exist. The land is not only the source of life-sustaining food; it is the base of our economy. It stores up energy and releases it when we need it. Knowing its capabilities, treating it according to its needs, using the proper methods of cultivating it, conserving its goodness- 
these form the base of the farmer's responsibility to the land.
But the man in the town or city is equally concerned, because no matter what his business may be he depends absolutely on the soil for what he eats. We need to co-operate to see that no productive land anywhere is being wasted. Every acre which goes out of production means that the pressure is increased on the remaining good acres. Unless we understand this, and do something effective about it, the people in barren countries will be driven to poverty, hunger and discord; and this is the condition of which strife is born. Canada is vitally interested in the world's food problem because she is one of the world's main surplus food producers. With a few others like the United States, Australia, New Zealand, Argentina and Brazil, her people have nothing to worry about so far as they themselves are concerned. But in the "want" countries it appears from statistics that about three-quarters of the people went to bed hungry last night, and for years of nights before that. The situation has its effect on the prospects of world peace. A hungry man does not look at life in the same way as he would if he were well fed. There is apathy in his outlook. Interest in public, political, social and cultural matters dies within him. He becomes centred on thoughts of self-preservation and preservation of his family at all costs.
The key to maintaining supplies of food and extending them is a program of soil conservation. Every grain of wheat, every egg, every pound of butter and every piece of beef depends upon an irreducible minimum of earth to produce it. The next few years will be critical in world history. It is mankind's biggest job to ward off world hunger. How to do this is a good subject for discussion in community meetings and forums, not only in country districts but in towns and cities. We are all in the same world boat, with limited supplies of food. Businessmen, housewives, farmers, transportation workers and others are all on one level when it comes to need of food and the preservation of world order.
The most critical danger is that we may forget how short we are of time. Today's crisis calls for an immediate uprising of the idea of conservation and development. Productivity of individuals needs to be increased by provision of modern scientific knowledge and modern tools, and by inspiring them so to work as to become a new source of wealth. There is a stirring need for laymen and women to work with the ABC's of the problem: advance education and industry; balance deficiencies with surpluses; conserve soil and resources.

The food which is produced from our farms, and any form of distribution, should be contributed by the nation as a whole and not by agriculture alone. In order to do this we should encourage our farmers in the great work that they are doing.

Mr. Speaker, in order to make it unanimous, and to keep continuity in this debate, I should like to join with the other hon. members who have spoken and congratulate the mover (Mr. Brown) and seconder (Mr. Demers) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should like also to join in the courtesies which have been extended to the new members, and to welcome them to their new seats in this house. At the same time may I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew) upon their elevation to positions not only of great honour but also of great responsibility in connection with the affairs of this country.
In the course of my remarks I intend to refer to several items which are of great concern to the people of my constituency. I shall first say a word on behalf of the old age pensioners. Almost every hon. member who rises in his place in this house says something about old age pensions, and I would not feel that I had done my duty in this respect, even at the danger of repeating what other hon. members have already said, if I did not make a plea on behalf of the old age pensioners in my constituency.
It is common knowledge to all members of the government, as well as to all other hon. members, that these old age pensioners are in destitute circumstances since the cost of living has increased to its present high level. This is a situation which has developed more through government policies than anything else. The pensioners are caught between the anvil of fixed income and the hammer of increasing food, rent and clothing costs; in short, the increasing cost of living. The same thing might be said of all Canadians in the lower-income brackets. They are virtually in the same position. Their incomes have not increased at the same pace that the cost of all the things they have to buy has increased.
The government has permitted this situation to continue and snowball down through the years despite the fact that it has had record surpluses, and despite the fact that it could have made other adjustments in income-tax levels, which would have brought some measure of relief to Canadian workers. It would appear that now some consideration is forthcoming, but the tragedy of it is that it is coming in an election year. No matter
The Address-Mr. Daniel how the government may seek to interpret it, any gesture towards income-tax concessions now can be considered as nothing short of political bribery.
The government has seen fit to give some indication that tax reductions definitely are forthcoming in the next budget. The hint was given in the throne speech itself in one paragraph, which referred to the high level of national prosperity, and the fact that the government would recognize this in its budgetary proposals. This reference in the throne speech constituted an amazing budget leak, but there appear to have been other leaks from the budget. I quote from a news item in the London Free Press of January 19 of this year:
Petrolla, January 19. A "sunshine" budget for Canadians in 1949, and in particular for the rural communities was forecast here today by Robert McCubbin, M.P. for Middlesex West and parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture.
Further on in the report in the Free Press of January 19 Mr. McCubbin said:
I realize there have been some hard feelings about income tax, but there is no need to fear.
I am sure that that is reassuring news. The report continues:
There is going to be some redress given to those in the lower income brackets. I am bothered by the high rate of taxation and the high cost of living and feel these are matters the government must take in hand. Officials at Ottawa admitted in 1945 that a $2,000 exemption was not too much.
Coming from a parliamentary assistant, a man whose position must be considered an official one, this statement of the hon. member for Middlesex West is almost as amazing as the paragraph in the throne speech. If this is not a budget leak, how else can it be interpreted? At least it is a major concession to have the member for Middlesex West confess that he is bothered by the high rate of taxation and the high cost of living. But for him to say that these are matters which the government must take in hand must strike the people of western Ontario as a belated recognition of "twin" responsibilties of the government, of which the government should have been aware, and with which the government should have dealt in years gone by. It is a little too late now for this government to make any pretence at seeking to come to grips with the problem of the high cost of living.
The fact that the high cost of living was causing all the people of Canada concern was recognized by the government itself a year ago when it set up a committee of this house to investigate what was then described as the recent increase in the cost of living. This committee sat all through the last session of parliament, and this work was furthered by a

The Address-Mr. Daniel royal commission on prices. Now in March of 1949 the government still has not received its report on what caused the recent high rise in the cost of living-"recent" in terms of 1947 and 1948.
As far as the government was concerned, I do believe this prices inquiry achieved its purpose. It removed from the floor of the house discussion of the high cost of living. It permitted the government to sidestep the greatest issue of the day. It is a little too late now for the hon. member for Middlesex West, or any other member of the government, to rise in the commons chamber, or to appear on the hustings, and say that the government now is aware that there is such a thing as a high cost of living, and that it intends to do something about it. The budget of 1949 is a little too late to attempt to salve the wounds inflicted on Canadian taxpayers during the past three or four years. Too little and too late. That summarizes the record of this government.
Incidentally, while I am discussing the subject of income tax concessions generally, I would like to make reference in particular to the latest income tax form. In looking over this form I see the same old questions as were on the form of years gone by, but the printing has become much smaller. They have finally come up with what they call a simplified form. There would appear to be some confusion however in the income tax branch as to what is meant by simplification. After looking over the latest form it would appear to me that simplification, in the hands of the income tax branch, means condensation. The form is condensed and contains tiny type which a chartered accountant friend of mine told me the other day he defied any man over thirty years of age to read. He does a great deal of work on these forms, and it is his prediction that by next year he will probably be next thing to blind. Would I be too inquisitive if I were to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) if he intends to supply Canadian taxpayers with bifocals, or glasses of some kind, so that they might at least be able to read what is on these forms?
While the radio tax is not a heavy one in itself, I believe it is the one which more than any other causes concern to the people of Canada. They are not so much interested in the amount of the tax as in the way it is collected. I know that around Christmas time some radio inspectors came to my home town. They did not even play fair with the people because, first of all, when they came to town they called upon radio salesmen and at the post office to find out whether John Jones or Dick Smith had bought his licence, or whether he had bought one last year. Then

all they had to do was to go around and knock on doors, scaring the poor housewife half out of her wits. She would think she was going to be arrested, because probably she had told her husband to get one, and he had told her to get one, with the result that neither of them got one. They find themselves in trouble, and a few days later it all comes out in the local paper, stating that John Smith has been charged with a breach of the law.
These people are no respecters of persons, because the millionaires are treated the same as other people, including widows and old people. I know that in about two days in Ingersoll about 120 were picked up. They had to pay fines, and then had to go out and buy a new radio licence.
Another tax to which I should like to refer briefly is the luxury tax on jewelry, one which has been brought forcibly to our attention within the last few days. Many jewelers have complained to me about the hardship it worked on them. They have pointed out how it has reduced sales in their particular line of business. For instance, a jeweler may have an article classed as a luxury by the department. However, one may walk up the street to a dealer who handles a cheaper range of goods, but one which is perhaps along the same line, generally. This man would handle cutlery, dishes, and all kinds of jewelry. At the second store one could purchase almost the facsimile of the article but at a ridiculously low price. But there is no tax on the article in the second store. Therefore I say the luxury tax on jewelry should be abolished immediately.
I should like to come back to the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin). I hope he does not think I am picking on him particularly. However, he seems to have been doing a good deal of talking around western Ontario in the last few weeks, so I cannot help quoting him.
Again I might cite the words of the hon. member for Middlesex West by way of proof that what this government has done to alleviate the situation for the Canadian taxpayers has been too little and too late. In an article which appeared in the London Free Press, he is quoted as telling the western Ontario agricultural institute that some families in Canada may be just as badly in need of clothes as those families in Britain receiving clothing parcels from this country. If families in Canada are in as sorry a plight as all that, then the member's own words constitute an indictment of this government's policies. It is true the hon. member was attempting to paint a glowing picture of the economic conditions in Britain, conditions

which he saw at first hand on a recent visit to that country. What the hon. member lor Middlesex West had to say on the subject has caused a great deal of consternation and controversy in this country and in Britain. The member's observations, as given to the western Ontario Jersey cattle club, were to the effect that Britain was well along the road to economic recovery, that everybody in Britain was working, was happy and was prosperous, that everybody had money and lots of it.
In another part of his speech the parliamentary assistant said that while in London he was unchaperoned. After reading what he has said, as reported in the Free Press, I am inclined to the belief that not only was he unchaperoned but that he was traveling incognito, and probably wearing rose-coloured glasses as well. Perhaps, after all, what he saw through those rose-coloured glasses was not really caviar, frogs' legs, quail on toast and all that kind of rich food he has spoken about, but rather just some more of the minister's applesauce. It will be recalled that the minister told us he was served applesauce during the two weeks he visited in Great Britain.
I know of no statement which has caused a greater injury to the harmony of Canadian-British relations than that of the hon. member for Middlesex West. It might be well to remind the hon. member that Britain today is getting major Marshall-plan assistance. Without this ERP, and other credits, Britain would be in a more difficult position than she is today. We all hope that she will be able to pull through in her battle of the dollar, as grim a fight as she staged during the war; but her battle has not yet been won. As far as we in this country are concerned, we cannot help wondering what will happen to Britain if and when ERP ceases; and, incidentally, we cannot help wondering what will happen to the level of our export trade to the United Kingdom if these funds suddenly should dry up.
Letters coming to private Canadians would indicate that the British people, rigidly rationed in the purchase of clothes and food, are having anything but a happy time. The rosy picture painted by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture left, I believe, an entirely false impression in the minds of many people. It was a disturbing impression, one which cannot but cause misunderstanding.
Another matter I should like to discuss is that of bovine tuberculosis. In 1939 a petition was circulated among the farmers of Oxford county asking the federal government to make the county an accredited area for the purpose of having our dairy herds
The Address-Mr. Daniel declared free of bovine tuberculosis. This petition evidently had the required number of signatures, but before a start was made on the test the war intervened and naturally the project was dropped for the time being.
At that time the amount paid to the owners of these T.B. reactors was set at $60 for a grade animal and $150 for a purebred, but for some unknown reason the government paid only two-thirds of this valuation, or $40 maximum for a grade animal and $100 for a purebred.
I believe that in the house this week the Minister of Agriculture, answering a question of the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Robinson), stated that the price of a purebred reactor was $100. I believe there must have been some mistake in that, because I am informed it is $150.

The price of a good grade cow was then about $100, so that if the animal reacted to the test and was condemned to slaughter, although the price of beef was very cheap the $40, or perhaps I should say $38, paid by the government was the maximum; and from there it grades down to as low as $10, $12 or $15. I have never heard of a farmer receiving the full $40. Although the price of beef was very cheap, the $40, or perhaps I should say the $38 paid by the government, plus the beef price of $50 average if the animal was passed by the veterinarian as fit for human consumption, made a total of $88. Of course, if the beast was declared useless the only receipt to the farmer for his $100 cow was the $38 government grant.
During the years of the war and since the prices of top grade dairy cattle have advanced to a high# of $250 to $300 per head, but the compensation has remained at the old level of $38 per head. The majority of these cattle in Oxford being of the dairy type, Holstein-Friesian, Jersey or Ayrshire, they never were classed as being particularly suitable for beef. The filet mignons that we sometimes get in Ottawa, and the other juicy steaks, do not as a rule come from beasts of the dairy type. Owing to the fact that they are tested at various stages of their lactation period they are usually rather on the thin side and in most cases are graded by the packing houses as canners or cutters or low-priced beef.
In spite of the comparatively high prices of all beef products the farmer receives only

The Address-Mr. Daniel an average of $100 to $150 provided the animal passes inspection. Suppose he gets $125 from the packer plus the government's $38, that makes a total of $163. Granted that the animal as a milk producer in her own stable is worth $250, that would leave a loss on the transaction of $87.
I realize that there are not many hon. members of this house who are acquainted with this situation. To the best of my knowledge there are only three in western Ontario who realize this situation. I spent the greater part of this morning trying to convince some of my colleagues on this side of the house that the farmer did not receive the full $60 or the full $150 mentioned the other day by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). The counties of Perth, Oxford and Middlesex East are the only counties in western Ontario where the test is presently going on.

The counties of Bruce, Huron, Brant and Lambton are applying for the test. I am sure that when those counties are being tested the minister will have many more resolutions coming in to him than he has had from the three counties I have mentioned, and I can assure you that to my knowledge he has had a great many from those three counties.
Many farmers have lost entire herds of from twenty or even eighty cattle or more. When that happens their whole economy is temporarily thrown off balance since they not only lose so much per head but in many cases find themselves unable to replace their herds, with the resulting loss of their monthly milk cheques. This is particularly a hardship on the young man who has just started up when he not only has to lose part of his capital investment but has no income with which to meet current expenses.
The Minister of Agriculture has received many resolutions during the past year from township councils, county councils and the federation of agriculture, but as yet he has made no change in the $38 compensation rate of many years' standing. The minister may remember the statement he made last February at Woodstock when he was the guest speaker at a meeting of the Oxford county federation of agriculture. On that occasion one of the persons who was attending the meeting stood up at the back of the hall and asked the minister a pertinent question in connection with an item we read a great deal about in the papers, something that is sometimes spread on bread. The minister answered that question in what I thought was a very good way.
To the best of my recollection he said that while he did not consider the question was

exactly fair, while he did not intend to commit himself, as a matter of fact he wanted to hear the debate on the matter on the floor of the house and after hearing that debate he would make up his mind as to any decision he might make. Therefore I am taking this opportunity to present to the Minister of Agriculture the position of the farmers of western Ontario and also the position of the farmers of eastern Ontario because I believe the testing will be started there very soon.
He suggested the other day that the government was considering making a change and I submit that either that change should go all across the board or the farmers should be paid for those reactors that become total losses. As it is now, for a $250 cow a farmer may receive only $38 plus $10 salvage for the hide, a total of $48. It is that fact that is causing a great deal of concern to the farmer.
I know of one herd of twenty-eight head in which fourteen were found to be reactors. Those cattle went into the fertilizer tank and the farmer received only $48 per head. If the government should come to a decision to pay more for these reactors I hope that it will be made retroactive so that the farmers of Oxford, Perth and Middlesex East may receive due consideration as well as the farmers in the new counties in which the test will be going on very soon.
In closing I should like to bring another matter to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). The other day the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Webb) asked the minister to look into a condition that existed in Brockville where Canadian National trains cross the main street and hold up traffic for considerable periods of time. No. 2 highway passes through the town of Ingersoll, and the railroad also passes through that town and cuts it in half practically in the middle. On the north side of the river is located one of,the largest factories in the town, employing possibly a thousand men. There are also two schools located there.
Three or four miles to the east of the town are located three limestone quarries. When the railroad is bringing in empty cars for the carriage of limestone products, crushed stone and so on, they are brought to Ingersoll and then put over what might be termed as the hump. Those who come from Winnipeg or Fort William will know how the wheat cars there are put over the hump for distribution. The result of this is that highwaj traffic is held up, perhaps not beyond the five-minute period, but sometimes it is nearly every other five minutes. I have seen the traffic held up as far back as two or three miles during the busy summer season.

The municipal council have taken up this matter at various times with the superintendent of the London division who has always been most courteous. He comes down to pay us a visit but the day he does come down the railway traffic seems to be very quiet. I presume he goes back to London and reports that the condition does not seem to be too bad, but the next day the traffic is twice as heavy. This is a situation which I wish the Minister of Transport would look into at his earliest opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising to take part in this debate at the present time is to refer to two or three problems which affect my constituency. The first has to do with the foreign exchange control board, and I am glad the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is in his seat. The second concerns a widow and her child, whose husband and father was killed in action in world war II. The third is the problem of the student veterans attending Queen's and other Canadian universities.
My first reference is to a seizure of $30 in United States funds, and my plea is on behalf of a young lady, Miss Renaud, who is employed at the aluminum company at Kingston. This lady was proceeding to Watertown, in company with two other ladies, on Sunday, July 27, 1947, to visit relatives. The other two ladies had gone to the bank on Saturday to obtain the necessary funds, and there they were supplied with the money and the forms. Miss Renaud had, over a period of time, accumulated an amount of $40 in United States funds, and therefore knew of no reason to go to the bank. When they arrived at the customs at Lansdowne, at the Ivy Lea bridge, the officials on duty asked what amount of currency these ladies were carrying. The other two had the form H, which they produced, while Miss Renaud voluntarily declared that she had $40 in United States money and $5 in Canadian funds.
What happened? She was astonished to learn that she could take with her only $10 in United States currency and $5 in Canadian money, since she did not possess a form H. This was something she had not known at all, and $30 in American money was taken from her. In passing I may say that she is only one of the many who, through lack of knowledge of the foreign exchange control regulations, have suffered monetary losses. She proceeded on her way with her friends, with a total of only $15 in money. On her return a couple of days later she asked for the $30 in American funds which had been left at the customs, and to her surprise was told that it had been confiscated and sent to Ottawa.
The Address-Mr. Kidd
As one who has lived along the border and who has been dealing with customs officials for over twenty-five years, I cannot speak too highly of the older officials, who are courteous and gentlemanly in meeting the public. Many are veterans of the first world war who entered the revenue department with the intention of making it their lifework. These officials now are asked to do a rather distasteful job for the foreign exchange control board, and are given no option in the matter. In order to keep up with the extra work caused by these erratic controls the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) has been obliged to increase the staff by many hundreds. These orders were put through so fast that there was no time to train the new staff, and as a result the public were confronted with personnel untrained and unfitted to perform duties which require great tact and courtesy. Many of these new officials considered that they had to be a little overzealous and superior in order to have their services recognized and retain their positions.
This loss of $30 by Miss Renaud meant a great deal to her. Friends acting on her behalf came to interview me, and since it comes under his department I wrote to the Minister of National Revenue under date of December 10, 1947. He replied on December 12, stating:
This is a matter over which I have no jurisdiction whatsoever. Our customs officers at border points in enforcing the foreign exchange regulations do so on behalf of the foreign exchange control board and report to them direct. The best I can do under the circumstances is to see that your representations are brought to the attention of the board. I am, therefore, passing your communication to the secretary, Mr. R. H. Tarr.
I then wrote a letter to the Minister of Finance, who confirmed the stand taken by the foreign exchange control board, stating that a great deal of publicity had been given to the requirements at the time. The foreign exchange control board also advised that the Minister of Finance made a statement on May 26, 1947, which was given wide publicity in the daily press and over the radio.
What are the facts? In the first place, order in council P.C. 2045 was passed on May 23, 1947. That was a Friday, and at that time the house was in session. No announcement was made in the house on either Thursday, Friday or Monday by the minister. Instead, he went on the air and made a statement. On Tuesday, May 27, four days later, as the result of a question asked by a member of this house at page 3465 of Hansard for that year, it leaked out that the regulations had been changed. At this point I want to take issue with the minister on his method of procedure. Once more we find that a confidential order in council was

No. This is a boy over sixteen. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is spending his time with a commission to deal with the high cost of living, when his time would be better spent in forming a commission to see that the taxpayers' money is

The Address-Mr. Kidd equitably distributed to those who are deserving and are justly entitled to it. I mean every word of that. I think the time has come for a check-up on the Canadian pension board. Some of the older members mean well, but they are in a rut and it is time they got out of it. If the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) were in his seat, I would say this to him. But as he is not, I would say to the acting leader of the house that I think the time has come when the Prime Minister should get the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) together and deal with cases like this. speechtext: I will tell the minister this. If anything happened to that mother today, the public trustee would take this child and look after it. That is their responsibility. This is really the responsibility of the Minister of National Defence. He was the O.C. of this man when he went overseas. The man was killed in action. It should not be for me, as a member of parliament, to fight this case. It is the responsibility of the Minister of National Defence under whom this man served. It is up to him to see that the men who served under him, and their dependents, are properly cared for.

speechtext: I would point out to the minister that appeals for men are being made. The department is going on the air, over the radio, and advertising. When a dependent of a boy who was killed overseas is refused assistance by a responsible minister of the crown, and when his dependents are not cared for, it is easily seen how this report spreads. It is doing the minister an injustice. This boy should be cared for.

I should like to make reference to the problem of the student veterans who are at present attending Queen's university and other universities in Canada.
The fourth annual national conference of student veterans was held on December 28, 29 and 30 last at Queen's university. Some

50 or 60 student veterans representing various universities across Canada attended. I had the honour to be present at their meetings.
A student veteran who fails to get a B average in the final examination of the year is cut off from the D.V.A. allowances of approximately $60, $90, $108 and so on a month, and therefore is automatically ineligible for assistance from the veterans university loan fund. This loan fund is one allowing every student on D. V. A. to borrow a maximum of $500 per annum or a total of $2,000 during his course. The loan is interest-free up to the January following graduation, and bears interest of five per cent per annum thereafter. The conditions for borrowing are as follows:
(a)	That need be proven.
(b)	That the student shall have completed successfully one year of university.
(c)	That the student in the opinion of the university loan board be of a responsible financial character.
(d)	That the student be still on the D.V.A. allowance.
A student veteran who fails to gain a B average, and who rewrites his examinations, is able to go back to the university and continue his studies, but he is not eligible for the D.V.A. allowance or the loan fund. At the present time there are 102 student veterans, out of a total student veteran population of 1,189, or roughly ten per cent, at Queen's university who have been cut off from both their allowance and the loan fund.
In some cases where the Department of Veterans Affairs has cut off the allowance of the student veteran, the university has come to his rescue by giving him a small loan from the university fund. The investment of the government in the education of veterans and the achievement of a higher standard of education in Canada will be jeopardized if student veterans are forced to discontinue their studies because of inadequate grants. A student veteran who is taking the course in medicine needs further assistance by the D.V.A. This is a six-year course, and the D.V.A. allowance does not cover this period of time.
These claims have already been brought to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs by the national council of student veterans, and it was also their intention to bring them before the committee on veterans affairs; but the minister stated that he was doubtful whether a parliamentary committee on veterans affairs would be appointed by parliament this year. To the minister I recommend that this committee be set up. This matter has already been brought to his attention by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green).

The case to which I have already made reference is not an isolated one. I wish to refer to another. We as members of parliament get the borderline cases. Here is another borderline case. I think these things should not happen at all. I should like to bring to your attention the case of a veteran of world war I, that of Private R. A. Baines, regimental number 814552, who enlisted with the 87th battalion on December 10, 1915, and was discharged in 1918 with a five per cent pension.
Mr. Baines was employed by the corporation of the city of Kingston. In July, 1947, Mr. Baines had a medical check-up by his family doctor; and he and his family were shocked to learn that he was in the advanced stage of T.B. His many friends naturally thought he would be taken into the D.V.A. hospital in Kingston. The D.V.A. hospital at that time had over one hundred T.B. cases and thirty-five to forty empty beds. When application was made for admission to this hospital, he was immediately refused on the ground that his discharge documents did not show T.B.
The medical health officer of Kingston found out that it might be possible to provide accommodation for Mr. Baines at the Kingston General hospital. This hospital is one of the finest 500-bed hospitals in Canada. At this time they had a section for some twenty-five or thirty T.B. patients, but it was filled and had a waiting list. Nevertheless the staff at the Kingston General hospital were prepared to provide accommodation for this man. The medical health officer thought it best for Mr. Baines to be placed in a T.B. hospital and endeavoured to have him sent to the Ontario T.B. hospital at Hamilton, but they were filled to overflowing and had quite a long waiting list. Finally, accommodation was provided for him at the Ontario T.B. hospital at Windsor, on July 19, 1947.
On July 21, 1947, the vice-president and secretary of the Canadian legion No. 9, Kingston, of which Mr. Baines was president, wrote to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, requesting permission be granted Mr. Baines for accommodation in the D.V.A. hospital at Kingston. I followed their letter up on July 23, 1947, with a letter to the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
In order for Mr. Baines to be near his family he was moved from the Windsor T.B. hospital and to the Kingston General hospital in January 1948. He was only there a few days when he died. The treatment received by this veteran of world war I was not good enough. This man was gassed in world war I, and there is no mistake his condition was due to war service. His widow, who is
The Address-Mr. Kidd not receiving a pension, should be receiving one. I respectfully request the Minister of Veterans Affairs to have this case looked into.
Here is the point I wish to make. We have a government hospital administered by the D.V.A., which has twenty or thirty empty beds. Here is a D.V.A. patient of world war I, but they will not let him enter that hospital because when they looked up his records they found no record of tuberculosis in his file. Who is responsible for it? Who is willing to take charge? The civil hospitals -the provincial hospitals at Hamilton and Windsor-were willing to take charge, which shows the weakness of the present set-up. These are borderline cases. I know that every hon. member gets these borderline cases, and they should be looked into.
The case of a nurse was brought to my attention. Again, the benefit of the doubt clause goes to the department or the government instead of the veteran. This nurse was taken on as A category in world war II and had two years' service. She was discharged as C category, with a 60 per cent pension. She was actually discharged with a 100 per cent disability due to a coronary heart condition, and is no longer able to carry on her duties in her profession. The pension board decided that her condition was a pre-enlistment one, and was aggravated by service.
The point I would like to bring out is this: Why was this nurse taken on as A category and continued to be in this category for one month, six months, twelve months, and even two years, but on her discharge was classed as a C category?
I am afraid that some of the junior medical officers who desire to remain in the service cater to the whims of the department and are not giving the breaks or the benefit of the doubt clause to the veterans.
